title: What is cash flow? Why the wealthy look at cash before profit.
subtitle: Profit shows efficiency on the statement. Cash flow shows financial capacity in reality.
openingQuestion: A company reports a 2 billion VND profit this quarter, yet has no money to pay wages. What is the most likely reason?
openingOptions: The company lost the money through internal corruption
Customers haven't paid yet, so the money is still a receivable
This cannot happen to a company that is profitable
The accountants miscalculated the profit figure
explanation: Accounting recognises revenue when the goods are delivered, but money only reaches the account when the customer actually pays. The gap between those two moments is where a great many businesses die: statements full of profit while there isn't enough cash for this month's wages. Experienced readers therefore read cash flow before profit - profit is an opinion built out of accounting estimates, whereas cash in the account either is there or isn't.

diagram.label: Meanwhile wages and materials still have to be paid
Only once the money arrives is there real cash flow

realWorldExample.description: Vinamilk reports profits in the trillions each quarter yet still takes short-term loans to pay for raw materials, because payments from supermarkets haven't come through in time.

quiz.question: What does positive cash flow mean?
options: More money came in than went out over the period
The company reported a positive accounting profit
The company has no outstanding borrowings left to repay
Revenue over the period grew against the previous one
quiz.explanation: Positive cash flow means that over that period you took in more than you paid out, whatever the accounting profit happened to be. It is the actual state of your cash health.

quiz.question: Who usually analyses cash flow most closely when assessing a business?
options: The marketing team when drawing up a sales plan
Lending banks and long-horizon investors
Internal accountants when preparing the year-end tax return
Customers when comparing product prices
quiz.explanation: A bank wants to know whether the company will have the money to service its debt. An investor wants to know whether it generates real cash or only paper profit. Both look at cash flow.

quiz.question: Scenario: You run an online shop. January: you sell 100 million VND of goods, the customer pays 70 million immediately and 30 million in 30 days. Stock costs 60 million, paid immediately. What is January's profit? What is January's cash flow?
options: Profit 10 million, cash flow 10 million (using cash received)
Profit 40 million, cash flow 40 million (forgetting the receivable)
Profit 40 million, cash flow 10 million (both figures right)
Profit 10 million, cash flow 40 million (the two reversed)
quiz.explanation: Profit = revenue − costs = 100 − 60 = 40 million. Cash flow = money in − money out = 70 − 60 = 10 million. The 30 million receivable reaches cash flow in February. This is the classic case: profit exceeds cash flow.

quiz.question: A business reports a 500 million profit and still goes under. What is the most plausible reason?
options: Corporate income tax came to more than the profit itself
The profit was miscalculated and the company is really loss-making
High profit always drags a matching negative cash flow with it
The profit sits in receivables, with no cash for debts falling due
quiz.explanation: Profit recognises revenue at the point of sale, while the money arrives later. Sell plenty to customers who pay late and paper profit climbs as the account drains - creditors do not wait for your customers to pay, and a business dies from running out of cash rather than from making a loss.

quiz.question: Scenario: That month you sell 100 million, the customer pays 70 million and owes 30 million. You pay out 80 million in cash. What was that month's cash flow?
options: Minus 10 million (= 70 − 80), despite 100 million of revenue
Plus 20 million (= 100 − 80, counting the unpaid amount)
Plus 70 million (= counting only what the customer has paid)
Minus 30 million (= treating the unpaid 30 as written off)
quiz.explanation: Cash flow counts only money that actually moved: 70 in, 80 out, minus 10 million. The profit statement for the same month still shows 100 million of revenue and 20 million of profit - both figures are correct, and they describe two different things.

keyTakeaways: Profit is an accounting figure; cash flow is real money in the account
Businesses go under because they run out of cash, not because a statement shows a loss
The wealthy manage cash flow first and profit second

practicePrompt.question: A business is profitable but short of cash. What is the most likely reason?
options: Profit is not the same thing as revenue
Customers have not paid in full yet
A profitable company doesn't need cash
Cash flow is always positive when a business is profitable
practicePrompt.explanation: Profit and cash flow do not always move together. Receivables and the timing of collection can leave a business short of cash while it is still profitable.

summary.keyIdea: Cash flow shows the real state of health; profit is an accounting figure.
summary.formula: Cash flow = money in − money out.
summary.commonMistake: Judging a business by its profit and ignoring its cash flow.
summary.action: In a business or your own finances, look at when money arrives and when it leaves to see the real picture.

application.title: Apply it now
application.message: Look back at a recent piece of income and ask: have I actually received the money, or is it still only revenue on paper?

sections.text: A company reports a 2 billion VND profit this quarter, yet has no money to pay wages. It sounds contradictory - but it happens more often than you would think, and it is why the wealthy always look at cash flow before they look at profit.
Profit and cash are two different things

Profit (under accrual accounting) is recognised the moment a sale is made, even though the customer hasn't paid. If a company sells a large volume on credit, the statement can show a large profit while there is almost no actual cash in the account. This is exactly how a 'profitable' company can be unable to meet payroll right now.
Why cash flow matters more than profit in the short run

Employees, suppliers and banks all have to be paid in real money, not in 'paper profit'. A business can report profits for several quarters in a row and still go under if it manages cash flow badly - a far more common cause of failure than trading at a loss.

items: Profit: an accounting figure, recognised at the point of sale whether or not the money has arrived
Cash flow: the money that actually entered and left the account over the period
Businesses go under because they run out of cash, not because a statement shows a loss

sections.label: How the wealthy think about it
sections.text: The wealthy and good CFOs track cash flow first, because that is what determines whether an organisation or a person survives the short run. Profit is a measure of long-run efficiency; cash flow is a measure of survival right now.

lines: When assessing anyone's financial health - your own included - the first question should be 'how much actual cash is left?', not 'what does the paper profit say?'.
